critique.good: CVE IDs and package names stay intact, version ranges have room to wrap, and the headers remain on one line. The 260px summary column avoids mid-word splits.
critique.problems: The initial viewport shows the ID and package but only a sliver of the version column. Readers must scroll considerably to assess severity and impact. Tall summary-driven rows also leave large empty areas under the short identification fields.
critique.cause: The 146px and 183px first columns consume 329px before affected versions begin. The 260px summary still requires many lines, while the full table is 850px wide.

critique.good: More of the affected-version column is visible initially, and the narrower table reduces horizontal travel. CVE IDs remain intact.
critique.problems: Package names break across lines, including the path-like name, while the narrow summary makes rows much taller and increases the separation between advisories. Severity and the summary still require scrolling.
critique.cause: The 125px package column provides only 104px for text, less than the 162px needed for the longest unbreakable name. The 160px summary provides 139px of text width, well below its longest unbreakable word.

critique.good: All five columns are within the viewport, so their order and relationship are immediately visible.
critique.problems: Identifiers, package names, version expressions and summaries fragment heavily. Extremely tall rows make it hard to scan or compare advisories, and most headers wrap.
critique.cause: Widths of 65–76px leave only 44–55px for text in each column. In particular, the 68px summary column forces extensive word splitting and drives the table's height.

critique.good: CVE IDs and package names stay on one line, and the version column gives constraints room to form readable groups. The wider summary keeps rows shorter than in the other designs.
critique.problems: The initial viewport shows almost none of the affected versions and none of the severity or summary. The tall rows also leave large empty areas under the identifiers, making comparison down the table laborious. The full table requires substantial horizontal scrolling.
critique.cause: The 146px CVE and 183px package columns consume 329px before versions begin. The 320px summary reduces wrapping but contributes substantially to the 870px total width.

critique.good: Identifiers and package names remain intact, and the narrower table reduces horizontal scrolling. Version tokens remain intact despite wrapping.
critique.problems: The initial view still reveals little of the version column. Constraints are broken into more lines, making each range harder to read as a unit. Very tall rows and extensive blank space in the first columns weaken the visual connection between adjacent advisories.
critique.cause: The 105px version column leaves 84px for text, while the 241px summary leaves only 220px; together they increase wrapping, with the summary driving much of the row height.

critique.good: More of the version column appears on first sight, package names remain intact, and the 140px version column keeps related constraints more compact than in r1B.
critique.problems: Every CVE ID wraps across two lines, making identifiers harder to scan and copy mentally. Severity and most version information still require scrolling, while tall summary-driven rows leave large blank areas beside the shorter cells.
critique.cause: The 105px CVE column provides only 84px of text width, below the 125px needed for a one-line ID. The 300px summary limits some wrapping but still produces tall rows and contributes to the 809px overall width.

critique.good: CVE IDs and package names remain intact, and the wider version column keeps more constraints together.
critique.problems: The first view shows only a sliver of affected versions, leaving severity and summary offscreen. The tall rows create large empty areas under the short identifiers and packages, making comparisons down the table slow.
critique.cause: The first two columns consume 329px of the 360px viewport. The 280px summary column drives the row heights, while the 140px version column adds to the horizontal scroll.

critique.good: CVE IDs and packages remain intact. The 300px summary reduces the table height compared with r2A without increasing the total width.
critique.problems: The initial view still reveals little of the version column, and version bounds wrap more frequently, making ranges harder to read as pairs. Severity and summary require substantial sideways scrolling.
critique.cause: The first two columns still use 329px. Reducing affected versions to 120px leaves 99px for text, while the summary sets most row heights.

critique.good: More of the affected-version column is visible initially, and its 140px width gives constraints more room. The shorter overall width reduces scrolling, while the 300px summary retains r2B's row heights.
critique.problems: Every CVE ID wraps, weakening the identifier column's scan rhythm, and the long package path splits. The version column is still cut off at the viewport edge; severity and summary remain offscreen.
critique.cause: The 105px CVE column provides only 84px of text width, and the 160px package column provides 139px, less than the longest package name needs.

understanding.purpose: Help readers identify security advisories affecting their dependencies and assess their severity and impact.
understanding.reading: Readers scan package names and version ranges to find relevant dependencies, then compare severity and consult the CVE ID and summary for details. Summary wrapping can set the row height, leaving room for other cells to wrap without necessarily making the row taller.
groups: CVE ID and severity identify and prioritize each advisory.
Package and affected versions work together to determine whether a dependency is affected.
Summary explains the impact of the advisory identified by the other columns.
keep_intact: CVE identifiers and package names, especially path-like names
Individual version numbers and comparison operators
may_wrap: Affected-version expressions at spaces or between separate constraints

bad.why: The package path breaks across lines as well as every CVE identifier. Saving 23px over r1C makes both identifying columns harder to scan for little gain at the viewport edge.

final.rationale: r3A keeps CVE identifiers and package names on one line, making the two columns visible at first sight useful for scanning. Its wider versions column helps keep related version bounds together, while the summary has enough width to moderate the very tall rows. The reader must scroll substantially to see severity and the summary, and the initial view reveals only the beginning of affected versions.

general: Give identifiers and related values enough room to remain easy to recognize and compare.
Allocate width to long prose with attention to the resulting row heights and the cost of horizontal scrolling.
Judge the initial viewport and the full scrollable table together.
specific: The 183px package column accommodates the long package path on one line.
The summary dominates row height, so its width materially changes the rhythm of the entire table.
At 360px, keeping both identifying columns intact leaves little of affected versions visible initially.

final.tradeoffs: r2B reduces horizontal scrolling by 40px while preserving one-line identifiers, but its narrower versions and summary columns wrap more. r1C and r3C expose more of affected versions initially, at the cost of wrapping every CVE ID.
final.uncertain: The ranges are approximate design tolerances, not browser-verified breakpoints; small width changes can alter wrapping. A designer prioritizing the amount of affected-version content visible on first sight could reasonably prefer r1C or r3C.

A.why: CVE IDs wrap, and the long package name breaks across lines. Large row heights leave extensive blank space in the visible columns, while the remaining fields require horizontal scrolling.

B.why: CVE IDs and package names stay intact, making the first two columns easy to scan. Affected versions begin at the viewport edge, and the tall rows make comparisons laborious.

C.why: CVE IDs and package names stay intact, and the rows are more compact than in B. The tradeoff is that affected versions and the remaining fields require horizontal scrolling.

D.why: Fitting all five columns into the viewport makes them extremely narrow. Extensive word and identifier splitting produces an exceptionally tall table that is difficult to scan.

E.why: Package names stay intact, but every CVE ID wraps and the visible rows contain large stretches of empty space. Most version information and the later columns require scrolling.

F.why: Package names remain intact and more of the version column is initially visible, but CVE IDs split over three lines and version ranges wrap heavily. The tall rows make scanning difficult.

reviews.unsure: The supplied images show only the left portion of the horizontally overflowing layouts, so I cannot fully assess the off-screen severity and summary columns or the total scrolling distance.

A.why: All five columns fit in the viewport, but the narrow columns fragment identifiers and prose, making the rows extremely tall and difficult to scan.

B.why: Packages are mostly readable and some version information appears initially, but every CVE ID wraps and the long package path splits. The tall rows leave substantial empty space in the visible columns.

C.why: CVE IDs and package names stay intact, making the first two columns easy to scan together. Only a sliver of affected versions appears in the viewport, and the rows are very tall.

D.why: Package names stay intact, but CVE IDs wrap and little of the affected-version column is visible initially. The tall rows create large gaps between entries.

E.why: More of the affected-version column is visible, but the narrow CVE column breaks each identifier across three lines, making advisories harder to recognize and compare.

F.why: CVE IDs and package names remain intact, and the visible rows are more compact than in C. Affected versions and the remaining columns require horizontal scrolling.

reviews.unsure: The supplied views of B–F show only the left portion of each table, so I cannot assess the widths or readability of the off-screen columns or the full horizontal scrolling cost.
